title: The Fourth Protocol
build: Bantam Software's US disk release, 1985 (C64 Preservation Project G64, marked good); five parts: the resident disk operating system and episode loader, the title and episode menu, and the three episodes

Draws a random jagged line, the trace of a voice print, across 24 steps from the point X, Y: each step moves four pixels right and up or down by a random amount around the line's middle (seeded from voice_seeds by A), drawing each segment in black (draw_line).

Copies four bytes of voice_seeds, the Ath set, to the random generator's state at $A8-$AB, so the same voice always draws the same trace.

Eight sets of four bytes for seed_random, one per voice: set 0 draws both the unknown caller and STIG NILSON, token 0, which is the answer the voice analysis leads to. The analysis accepts people 0 to 11; for 8 to 11 the sets run on into random_below's code, whose bytes serve as seeds just as well.
The next value of the random generator at $A8-$AA (shifted eight bits, its feedback the bits picked by AND $48), repeated until it is less than A; returns it in A.

Draws a line from ($DE, $E0) to ($E1, $E2) a pixel at a time, with a short delay at each: the step in x and y worked out as fixed-point fractions of the longer side (line_steps), each pixel's bit cleared (plot_pixel), which shows its cell's background colour: red in the voice-print windows, whose colour byte is $F2.

Works out the steps for draw_line: whichever of the x and y distances is longer moves by one pixel a step, and the other by its share, the distance divided by the longer one (divide), both negated when the line goes left or up.

Sir Anthony Plumb's six questions (number 3's routine, when 12377563 is dialled): who is the British traitor, his contact's nationality, his alias, his real name, the proof and where it happened. Each answer is looked up as a word (ask_word) and compared with its token; a wrong one clears plumb_all_right ($1957).
Traitor: token $29, DEREK or FAULK(NER).

Proof: token $2B, FINGERP(RINT).
Where: token $2C, GAZA.

Counts frames in $1936/$1937; at $3840, 14,400 frames, the day ends: the day number goes up, the date (BCD, $1934) and month ($1935) with it, the calendar is redrawn, and the endings tested. Then the frame count starts again from 0, today's events run (run_todays_events), the watchers report (daily_surveillance) and the allowance of watchers is worked out again (daily_watchers). At 50 frames a second a day lasts 4 minutes 48 seconds.
A new day.

The bell's rhythm and the call timer, every frame: when the bell's own count ($193F) runs out, its phase ($1942) goes round 0 to 3: on for 22 frames, off for 3, on for 22, off for 80, the double ring of a British telephone.
Phases 0 and 2 ring, 1 is the short gap, 3 the long one.

Time up: the bell stops.

No call waiting: the next one in the tray, if any.
It rings, for up to 1,920 frames (38 seconds).

The short gap, 3 frames.
The long gap, 80 frames.
The gap's length, and the gate off.
Voice 3's gate off ($D412 = $14: triangle and ring modulation).
Starts the bell: phase 3 with 3 frames to run, so the first ring comes at once; voice 3's sustain at full and its pulse low byte set.
